extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political economy; policymakers and historians of economic thought
extracted.subtask_short: analysis of mercantile and agricultural systems
extracted.subtask_description: Close exposition and critique of 18th-century mercantile (commercial) regulations and an outline of the agricultural school of political economy, describing legal restraints, economic effects, and the classification of economic actors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bond and record for inland purchases of wool within 15 miles of sea
rubrics_metrics.description: No person within fifteen miles of the sea can buy any wool before he enters into bond to the king that no part of the wool which he shall so buy shall be sold by him to any other person within fifteen miles of the sea; entry of the name and abode of the person to whom they are sold, and of the place to which it is intended they should be carried.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If wool is found carrying towards the sea unless entered and security given as aforesaid, it is forfeited, and the offender also forfeits 3s. for every pound weight. If any wool not so entered is laid within fifteen miles of the sea it must be seized and forfeited; any claimant must give security to the exchequer that if cast upon trial he shall pay treble costs, besides other penalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Port entry requirement before coast-wise carriage (within five miles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every owner who carrieth any wool to any port or place on the sea coast to be transported by sea must first cause an entry thereof to be made at the port from whence it is intended to be conveyed, containing weight, marks, and number of the packages, before he brings the same within five miles of that port.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Penalty: forfeiture of the wool and also of horses, carts, and other carriages; and suffering the usual additional penalty (as with other laws against exportation) including an additional 3s. per pound where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shearer’s-home carriage certificate procedure (exception to five-mile rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exception allowing a person to carry his wool home from the place of shearing even if within five miles of the sea, provided that within ten days after shearing he certifies under his hand to the next customs officer the true number of fleeces and where housed; and that he does not remove the wool without certifying his intention three days before removal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an indulgence to avoid unduly preventing small-scale movement of fleeces; failure to follow the certificate/notice procedure would expose the wool to the same penalties as other un-entered wool.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bond for coast-wise carriage to specified landing port
rubrics_metrics.description: Bond must be given that the wool to be carried coast-ways is to be landed at the particular port for which it is entered outwards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If any part is landed without the presence of an officer, one incurs forfeiture of the wool and the additional penalty of 3s. for every pound weight (in addition to other forfeitures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Export prohibition vs. export tax as policy standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Absolute prohibition of exportation of wool is criticised; the text proposes a tax of five or ten shillings upon exportation as an alternative that would produce revenue and hurt growers less than prohibition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument-level guidance: a moderate export tax would still advantage domestic manufacturers (by making foreign purchase more expensive) while producing sovereign revenue and reducing smuggling and the harms of total prohibition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Export prohibition extended to fuller’s earth and similar clays
rubrics_metrics.description: Exportation of fuller’s earth (fuller’s clay) and tobacco-pipe clay has been subjected to nearly the same penalties as the exportation of wool, due to resemblance and fear of mislabelling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy rationale: materials seen as necessary inputs for domestic manufactures were often restricted to prevent their leaving the country, even if they differed technically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on export of raw hides and tanned leather (with exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: By statute (13th & 14th Charles II chap. 7) the exportation not only of raw hides but of tanned leather, except in the shape of boots, shoes, or slippers, was prohibited; later statutes allowed tanners to be exempt upon payment of a small tax and drawbacks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subsequent modifications: tanners obtained exemption by paying one shilling per 112 lb and a drawback of two-thirds of excise duties; all manufactures of leather may be exported duty free and exporters get drawback of excise when exported without further manufacture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction of exportation of partially manufactured goods and materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Restraints (prohibitions or taxes) are commonly applied to goods that are partially but not completely manufactured (incomplete manufactures) to protect domestic manufacturers who claim the right to finish the commodity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include woollen yarn, worsted, white cloths (duty on export), watch-cases, clock-cases, and dial-plates; effect is to reserve downstream stages of manufacture to domestic makers and raise foreign competition barriers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical metal export prohibitions and selective exemptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Older statutes prohibited exportation of nearly all metals; later acts (5 W & M chap.17, 9 & 10 W III chap.26) exempted iron, copper, mundic, and permitted exportation of copper bars, but unmanufactured brass and certain metal forms remained prohibited while metal manufactures could be exported duty free.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pattern: raw/unmanufactured strategic materials were often restrained while finished manufactures were permitted to leave duty-free to encourage domestic industry in finished goods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Export duties on materials of manufacture when not prohibited
rubrics_metrics.description: Where exportation of materials is not absolutely prohibited, it is frequently subjected to considerable duties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory examples and the book of rates show how duties were used to discourage export without outright prohibition; duties sometimes made export economically unviable or tempted smuggling.

rubrics_metrics.name: 8 Geo. I. chap.15 exception list for duty-free export of manufactures
rubrics_metrics.description: The statute rendering manufactured goods duty free on export excepted a long list of materials/incomplete manufactures (alum, lead, tin, tanned leather, wool, white woollen cloths, cards, coals, etc.), leaving them subject to old duties and old subsidies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These exceptions demonstrate a legal distinction between finished manufactures (duty-free) and materials/instruments/incomplete manufactures (still taxed) — a policy aimed at keeping raw materials for domestic use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Import-exempt dyeing drugs with re-export duty to discourage re-export
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain foreign dyes/drugs (e.g., gum senega/gum arabic) were exempted from import duties to favor domestic manufacturers, but subjected to a small poundage duty on re-exportation; later, re-export duties were raised dramatically to discourage re-export and attempt to keep supplies for domestic industry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This policy sought to encourage importation for domestic use while preventing those materials from being resold abroad at low prices; it often produced smuggling and counterproductive effects, prompting later adjustments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confine export trade of colonial productions to Great Britain with heavy export penalties
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutes (e.g., 5 Geo. III chap.37) confined exportation of colonial products such as gum senega from African dominions to Great Britain and subjected them to severe restrictions, forfeitures, and high re-export duties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical consequence: enormous re-export duties incentivized smuggling and clandestine trade; later statutes reduced duties in response to evasion and economic pressure (e.g., 14 Geo. III chap.10).

rubrics_metrics.name: Manipulation of duty rates to favor domestic manufacturers (beaver example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjustments in duties (e.g., beaver skins reduced import duty but export duty raised substantially without drawback) were used to try to confine the supply and price to domestic manufacturers, often to the detriment of foreign suppliers and colonial producers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrates how duty-setting was used strategically by manufacturers to create effective monopolies and extract advantage from colonial/domestic supply chains; such measures invite smuggling and market distortions.

rubrics_metrics.name: High duties on export of instruments of trade and coal
rubrics_metrics.description: Exportation of instruments of trade (frames/engines for knitting, utensils for cotton/linen/wool/silk manufactures) is prohibited often under heavy penalties; coal export duties could exceed the original commodity value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Penalties range from forfeiture of goods to large monetary fines (some half to informer). Such extreme restraints aim to prevent dissemination of production capability but can be economically inefficient and provoke evasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Penalties for exporting frames/utensils and liability of ship masters
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutes impose forfeiture of prohibited utensils and monetary penalties (e.g., two hundred pounds each) on persons exporting and on masters of ships who knowingly allow such items to be loaded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These dual liabilities aim to deter both exporters and transporters; the large fines show the seriousness with which states sought to prevent transfer of manufacturing tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Penalties for enticing artificers to go abroad and restrictions on expatriate artificers
rubrics_metrics.description: By statute (5 Geo. I chap.27; 23 Geo. II chap.13) a person convicted of enticing an artificer to go abroad to practice or teach his trade faces heavy fines and imprisonment (rising between first and subsequent offences); artificers may be obliged to give security not to go abroad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Penalties escalated across statutes (first offence fines up to 100 pounds and three months imprisonment; later increased to 500 pounds and 12 months, then 1000 pounds and two years). Courts could require security and imprison until security given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences for artificer abroad not returning after warning
rubrics_metrics.description: If an artificer who has gone abroad and is exercising his trade does not return within six months after warning by ministers/consuls/secretary of state and thereafter abide in the realm, he is declared incapable of taking legacies, being executor/administrator, taking lands, forfeits all lands/goods/chattels, declared an alien and put out of king’s protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This extreme statutory sanction was designed to deter skilled craftsmen from emigrating with knowledge; it carries civil disabilities and forfeiture of property besides loss of legal status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normative principle: consumption as the ultimate purpose of production
rubrics_metrics.description: Assertion that 'consumption is the sole end and purpose of all production; and the interest of the producer ought to be attended to, only so far as it may be necessary for promoting that of the consumer.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a normative criterion to evaluate mercantile regulations: policies that privilege producers at consumers' expense (through higher prices, taxes, or enforced monopolies) are condemned as contrary to public interest and justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of mercantile system privileging producers over consumers
rubrics_metrics.description: Mercantile laws often sacrifice consumers’ interest to producers’ interest — restraints on importation, bounties on exportation, and colonial monopolies burden home consumers with higher prices and the costs of empire (defence and debt).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy evaluation: one should account for the full fiscal and welfare costs (e.g., wars and debts to maintain colonies) when judging claimed benefits to producers; small producer gains rarely offset large consumer and fiscal costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agricultural system classification of economic actors
rubrics_metrics.description: The agricultural system divides economic actors into three classes: proprietors of land; cultivators (farmers and country labourers) called the productive class; and artificers, manufacturers, and merchants called the barren or unproductive class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This classificatory rubric underpins claims that land/its produce is the sole source of national revenue and wealth, a position the author examines critically as largely theoretical and not historically adopted as state policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proprietors’ contribution described as 'ground expenses'
rubrics_metrics.description: Proprietors contribute to annual produce by expenses on improvement (buildings, drains, inclosures, ameliorations) which enable cultivators to raise greater produce and thus pay greater rent; such expenses are termed ground expenses (depenses foncieres).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These expenses are treated as capital yielding interest/profit to proprietors in the form of advanced rent; recognition of landlord investment as productive within the agricultural system’s accounting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivators’ contributions: original and annual expenses and replacement requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Cultivators contribute via original expenses (instruments, stock, seed, maintenance during early occupancy) and annual expenses (seed, wear and tear, maintenance of servants/cattle). The produce remaining after paying rent ought to replace original expenses within reasonable time and annually replace annual expenses plus ordinary profits of stock.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This sets a standard for what constitutes adequate farming returns: net produce must cover capital recovery and normal returns; it is an accounting rubric for evaluating agricultural profitability and sustainability.
